extracted.intended_audience: newspaper reporters and journalism students who cover court news
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing news stories about judicial procedure and court proceedings (police court, criminal trials, civil suits, probate, appeals), focusing on what to include and how to present it accurately and attractively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type of story
rubrics_metrics.description: All forms of judicial procedure are included under court news, stories of this class cover such matters as police court news, criminal trials, civil suits, divorce suits, bankruptcy, wills and other probate court matters, decisions of higher courts, and findings of judicial officers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Since much court news is routine, the matter-of-fact informative news story is a frequent medium for presenting it. Examples and cross-references: 'Supreme Court Decision', 'Opinion of Attorney General', 'Criminal Court', 'Municipal Court', 'Forgery Case'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose — fair and accurate publicity
rubrics_metrics.description: To give fair and accurate publicity to significant phases of the administration of justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court proceedings are public matters; the writer should direct the reader's attention to details that (1) are significant to him personally, (2) affect the interests of the community, and (3) relate to the welfare of society as a whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publicity's civic function (deterrence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Wide-spread publicity given by newspapers to punishment of wrong-doers tends to deter others from similar illegal acts and thus aids the chief object of punishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructive stories of crime and criminal trials can have social benefit by deterring crime; the reporter should be aware of this public-service aspect when covering court news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid sensationalism and anti-social influences
rubrics_metrics.description: Court stories that play up disgusting or scandalous phases to gratify morbid taste are destructive or anti-social.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not exploit disgusting details of criminal or divorce cases for morbid curiosity; avoid coverage that creates harmful public sentiment or indulges sensationalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not 'try the case in the newspaper' or publish inadmissible evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspapers should not undertake to prove the innocence or guilt of an accused by printing whatever evidence they can secure, even though some of it would be excluded from the trial under the rules of evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishing excluded or prejudicial evidence can create public opinion and arouse feeling so as to prevent the accused's having the fair trial to which he is entitled; maintain respect for due process and evidentiary rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of material — find significance in legal technicalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Find matters of general significance and interest, particularly when they are buried in legal technicalities and verbiage, and present them clearly and attractively without sacrificing accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Main problem is extracting salient, significant phases from legal documents and technical language; the successful court story presents these clearly and attractively while remaining accurate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone/medium — matter-of-fact but potentially interesting
rubrics_metrics.description: Because much court news is of a routine character, the matter-of-fact informative news story is a frequent medium for presenting it; this does not imply the news is necessarily dry and uninteresting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By bringing out salient and significant phases, decisions, legal documents, wills, bankruptcy cases, and criminal/civil suits, the facts can be made of interest even to the casual reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of human-interest elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Criminal and civil cases often have a strong human interest element that, if rightly developed, may be a valuable part of the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Little comedies and tragedies of police court are favorite subjects for entertaining and appealing human interest stories; use human elements to engage casual readers when appropriate and relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of the body of a court story
rubrics_metrics.description: The body of court news stories usually consists of summaries of arguments, decisions, testimony, or legal documents, or of excerpts from them, with the necessary connective material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In some instances the story may be largely a history of the case or of the persons involved. Use connective material to make excerpts and summaries read coherently for a general audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead selection — determined by status of the case
rubrics_metrics.description: The lead is usually determined by the status of the case; any one of the important points may be made the feature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose as the lead whichever important point (verdict, sentence, decision, testimony, etc.) most fits the current status and newsworthiness of the case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation of testimony — three acceptable forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Testimony in news stories is given in one of three forms: (1) the question indicated by 'Q' and the answer by 'A,' both question and answer given in one paragraph without quotation marks, (2) the question and the answer in quotation marks, each followed by the necessary explanatory matter and each in a separate paragraph, (3) a summary of the testimony of each witness in indirect quotation form, with the name of the witness at or near the beginning of the first sentence of the summarized testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select the testimony format that best fits clarity, space, and accuracy needs; be consistent and make clear who said what, especially when summarizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include the verdict and conditions under which it was rendered
rubrics_metrics.description: Important detail: the verdict and the conditions under which it was rendered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State the verdict clearly and note any circumstances that affected how or why it was rendered (e.g., plea, jury difficulty, special circumstances).

rubrics_metrics.name: Report the sentence imposed
rubrics_metrics.description: Important detail: the sentence imposed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide specifics of punishment (term, fines, probation, alternatives) and any modifiers or special conditions attached to the sentence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain the decision rendered and its significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Important detail: the decision rendered and its significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For rulings and higher-court decisions, explain both the immediate outcome and broader legal or social implications for readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Highlight important testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: Important detail: important testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarize or quote testimony that materially affects the case, using the appropriate testimony format and indicating source credibility or contradictions when relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide net results of the day's proceedings in a trial
rubrics_metrics.description: Important detail: net results of the day's proceedings in a trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reporting multi-day trials, summarize what was accomplished during the day's session (what evidence was introduced, witnesses heard, procedural rulings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Give the history of the case or action
rubrics_metrics.description: Important detail: the history of the case or action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include relevant background so readers understand context: prior proceedings, key events, chronology of the dispute or crime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report provisions of a will when relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: Important detail: provisions of a will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When covering probate or will contests, summarize material provisions and explain their significance to beneficiaries or public interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: State liabilities, assets, and cause in bankruptcy cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Important detail: liabilities, assets, and cause in bankruptcy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide clear summary of the debtor's financial condition and reasons for bankruptcy that are material to public understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report the award or finding
rubrics_metrics.description: Important detail: the award, or finding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In civil suits and administrative findings, state the award/amount or finding and its immediate consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain the grounds on which a suit is based
rubrics_metrics.description: Important detail: the grounds on which a suit is based.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarize the legal basis or claims of the plaintiff(s), including key allegations or causes of action so readers can grasp the dispute's nature.
